blog.title: H3: Uber’s Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index

summary: A ride app has to find a nearby car fast. Uber’s H3 grid covers the world with hexagons that nest inside each other at 16 zoom levels, and Uber says it measures supply and demand per hexagon to calculate surge pricing.

hook.teaser: How does a ride app find a nearby car without checking every car in the city?

media.alt: A city map that flips from a square grid to a honeycomb. A rider and a car sit in one hexagon, tagged with the same cell.
One big hexagon zooms in and becomes seven smaller hexagons, like a magnifying glass on honeycomb.

blocks.kicker: Real world / A picture story in four parts
blocks.title: Honeycomb over the map

chapters.title: Who is closest?
chapters.caption: A rider opens the app, and the app must find the nearest car. If it checks every car one by one, the job gets slower as the city grows. In a small town there are 3 cars to check. In a big city there are 12.

media.alt: A rider checks three cars in a small town, then twelve cars in a big city. Checking each car takes longer as the city grows.

chapters.title: Tile the world
chapters.caption: Lay a honeycomb over the whole map. Every spot lands in one hexagon, and each hexagon gets an ID. Uber says hexagons suit this job: a hexagon has one distance to all six neighbors, while a square has two.

media.alt: A city map with a honeycomb laid over it. Every spot falls into one hexagon, and a rider sits in one of them.

chapters.title: Zoom in, it splits
chapters.caption: The grid has levels, like zoom on a map. Zoom in one level and each hexagon splits into about seven smaller ones. Each finer level covers about one-seventh of the area above it. The fit is only approximate: finer cells only approximately fit inside their parent.

media.alt: One big hexagon splits into seven smaller ones; the middle cluster is zoomed in once more to show it splitting again.

chapters.title: Counting the cells
chapters.caption: The post gives design numbers, not speed tests. In its worked example, a map of California at resolution 6 needs 901 hexagons in the compact list, where the full list has 10,633. That is one example, not a benchmark. The picture is a schematic, not to scale. See the example in the post ↗

media.alt: Two lists of hexagons for the same map: a full list of many small cells, and a compact list with fewer, bigger cells.

blocks.kicker: Real world / Under the hood / A comic in three strips
blocks.title: How the honeycomb works
blocks.deck: Read each strip from left to right. The pictures move. Our story is one rider looking for one car.
blocks.howTo: Where a strip shows the post's claim, its stamp says so. The post's key numbers are in the evidence box at the end. The drawings are made up to explain the idea.

strips.title: Why hexagons, not squares?
strips.grownUpWords: hexagonal grid, neighbor distance (squares have two)

panels.caption: A square has four sides and four corners. Its neighbors touch it at a side or only at a corner.

media.alt: Nine squares. The four sides are green and the four corners are yellow. A corner neighbor sits further away.

panels.caption: A corner neighbor is further away than a side neighbor. The post's H3 section says squares have two distances, which makes comparing neighbors messy.

media.alt: One hexagon in the middle with six green neighbors, all the same distance away.

panels.caption: A hexagon has six neighbors, and the post's H3 section says each one is the same distance away. One distance, so it is easy to compare.

media.alt: A small honeycomb with arrows of equal length to each neighbor. A looker says: same distance, every neighbor.

strips.title: Zoom in, it splits in seven

panels.caption: One big hexagon covers a whole neighborhood. Its ID names that cell.

media.alt: One big hexagon cell. A looker asks what is inside it.

panels.caption: Zoom in, and the post's H3 section says each small one covers about one-seventh of the big one, so about seven fit in its place. It is only approximate: the cells do not fit perfectly.

media.alt: A faded big hexagon becomes seven smaller hexagons after an arrow.

panels.caption: Zoom again, and every small one splits too. Tiny cells, same honeycomb rule.

media.alt: A magnifying glass shows seven tiny hexagons inside one small cell. A looker says: zoom in again.

panels.caption: A rider taps “Find a car.” The rider sits in one hexagon. A car in the same hexagon carries the same cell ID.

media.alt: A rider and a car stand in the same hexagon, which is tagged with one cell ID.

panels.caption: No car in the same hexagon? The app looks in the hexagons touching it next. Try each one in turn.

media.alt: A rider stands in an empty hexagon. Its six neighbors pulse one by one, and a car is in one of them.

panels.caption: Found one! Still nothing? The app keeps searching farther out, step by step.

media.alt: A rider waves at a car in a neighboring hexagon. A bubble says: found one, and the car goes VROOM.

facts.text: base cells laid over the whole Earth, ten per face of an icosahedron (a 20-sided solid). Some cells belong to more than one face.

media.alt: A globe covered in a honeycomb of hexagons.

facts.text: pentagons, one at each corner of the icosahedron. The post says its authors chose to add them.

media.alt: A grid of twelve pentagons among the hexagons.

facts.text: The size of one cell’s ID. Each cell is named by a single 64-bit integer, one whole number.
